clinicalPearls: Combination of a tonic (Adie) pupil with diminished or absent deep tendon reflexes, most often in young adult women
The affected pupil is large (mydriatic), reacts poorly and slowly to light, but constricts slowly and tonically to sustained near effort, giving light-near dissociation
Vermiform (segmental) movements of the iris margin may be visible on slit-lamp examination
Denervation supersensitivity is demonstrated by constriction to dilute pilocarpine that would not affect a normal pupil
Usually benign and idiopathic, reflecting damage to the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves
Patients may notice anisocoria, photophobia, or difficulty focusing at near from accommodative paresis
When accompanied by segmental anhidrosis it overlaps with Ross syndrome
Management is reassurance and symptomatic measures; no specific treatment reverses the pupillary abnormality
reference.pathophysiology: Holmes-Adie syndrome results from postganglionic parasympathetic denervation of the iris sphincter and ciliary muscle, usually from injury to the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves. Acutely the pupil is dilated and poorly reactive; with aberrant reinnervation, fibres originally destined for the ciliary muscle misdirect to the iris sphincter, producing the characteristic slow, tonic constriction to near effort and light-near dissociation. Denervation renders the sphincter supersensitive to dilute cholinergic agonists. The associated hyporeflexia reflects an accompanying degeneration of dorsal root ganglion neurons. The cause is usually unknown, although viral or autoimmune mechanisms have been proposed.
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination for vermiform iris movements and light-near dissociation
Dilute pilocarpine test to demonstrate cholinergic supersensitivity
Syphilis serology when an Argyll Robertson pupil is a consideration
Review of drug and eye-drop exposure to exclude pharmacological mydriasis
Autonomic testing where a wider dysautonomia such as Ross syndrome is suspected
redFlags: A painful dilated pupil with ptosis or an eye-movement deficit suggesting a compressive third nerve palsy or aneurysm
Acute severe headache accompanying the pupillary change
Progressive or bilateral involvement with systemic features
reference.prognosis: Holmes-Adie syndrome is benign; the tonic pupil may remain enlarged or become smaller over years (the 'little old Adie's pupil'), and the main consequences are cosmetic anisocoria and near-vision symptoms rather than serious morbidity.
pitfalls: Confusing the tonic pupil with a dangerous third nerve palsy or aneurysmal mydriasis
Overlooking light-near dissociation, the key clinical sign
Attributing the anisocoria to pharmacological causes without proper testing
Missing associated anhidrosis that would indicate Ross syndrome
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Reassure that the condition is benign and requires no disease-modifying treatment
Manage photophobia and glare with tinted lenses or sunglasses, and correct accommodative near-vision difficulty with reading spectacles
Consider dilute pilocarpine drops to constrict the tonic pupil where anisocoria is cosmetically troublesome
Review drug and eye-drop exposure and check syphilis serology where an Argyll Robertson pupil is a consideration
Monitor for evolution into a wider dysautonomia such as Ross syndrome, with autonomic assessment where symptoms suggest it
Refer to ophthalmology or neurology to confirm the diagnosis and follow up the associated hyporeflexia
